claims.text: High-entropy alloys typically contain at least five principal elements, each at an atomic concentration between 5% and 35%.
The target systems include multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and disordered liquid states near their melting points.
Conventional EAM references in TOR-TILD cannot capture the configurational diversity of an ab initio multicomponent liquid.
The inability of EAM references to represent liquid configurations causes significant thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The conventional EAM reference should be replaced by an actively learned high-dimensional neural-network or comparable machine-learning interatomic potential.
The machine-learning potential should be trained on diverse ab initio configurations from both solid and highly disordered liquid phases.
A high-dimensional machine-learning potential can incorporate many-body correlations and a wider range of local atomic configurations than the EAM reference.
Training on extensive solid and liquid ab initio data will make the reference sample the target atomic-environment phase space more faithfully.
More faithful sampling by the reference will improve phase-space overlap with the ab initio target.
Improved reference-target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The machine-learning reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by roughly 50% relative to TOR-TILD's conventional EAM references.
The improved reference will yield closer agreement in free-energy differences, including the free energy of melting.
The proposed method is applicable to refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature conditions.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at temperatures at or near the alloy melting point.
Successes of related machine-learning references in elemental and binary systems support the feasibility of the proposed improvement.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on training-data quality, model architecture, and hyperparameter optimization.
Failure to achieve an approximately 50% reduction in path mismatch, or failure to improve phase-space overlap, would falsify the hypothesis.
